title: Farid: the crows and the eyes
hook: crows may peck the whole body, but spare the two eyes that hope to see the Beloved (Farid salok, ang 1382)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid on the Creator in creation. Your line was whom shall I call bad. Did you get through the day without filing anyone under bad? Today, one of the strangest, most beautiful couplets in the whole Granth. Day two hundred sixty-one.

Have you ever waited so long for someone that you stopped caring about everything else? The coffee went cold. You forgot to eat. Your back ached from standing at the window. You'd have given up almost anything, but not your view of the road, the one place they'd appear. Farid has a picture of that kind of waiting, and it's not gentle. It's a body, worn out, with crows landing on it. And one small, fierce request. Today, Farid: the crows and the eyes.
screen: `THE COFFEE WENT COLD.` → `STILL AT THE WINDOW.` → `ONE THING YOU WON'T GIVE UP.`

segments.voice: Near the end of Farid's saloks, on Ang 1382, he paints himself as someone who has waited a whole life for God. In paraphrase: my body has dried to a skeleton, and crows peck at my palms; and still the Lord hasn't come. Look at the fate of this servant. Then the next salok, in the original: kaagaa karang dhandholiaa sagalaa khaaiaa maas; e due nainaa mat chhuhau pir dekhan kee aas. Crow, you've searched my skeleton and eaten all my flesh. But please don't touch these two eyes. I still hope to see my Beloved. It's shocking at first: crows, a skeleton. But it's the bride and her longing again, birha, which we met two weeks ago, told in the starkest picture Farid could find. Everything can go: comfort, youth, strength, the body itself. The one thing he asks to keep is the ability to look for the one he loves. Many readers hear something more in the crows. They can stand for all the things that pick at a life: worries, desires, the years, the world's small bites. Let them take what they take. Just keep the eyes, the part of you that's still turned toward God, or toward what's good, still hoping. In Sufi and Punjabi poetry, pir means the beloved, the husband, and for Farid, God. And aas means hope. So the couplet ends where Farid always ends: not in despair, but in hope, stubborn and alive, while there are still eyes to see.
screen: `A BODY WORN TO BONE.` · `KAAGAA — CROW, TAKE THE REST.` · `BUT SPARE THE TWO EYES.` · `AAS — HOPE TO SEE THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `SPARE THE EYES.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window or up at the sky; if not, close your eyes and picture it. Let the worries of the day be the crows. They can peck at what they like for a minute. Keep your gaze soft and open, looking up, with a little longing in it: for God, if you pray, or for goodness, peace, someone you love. Just look, and hope. The bell holds the time.
Farid. Here, his salok: crow, take my flesh, but spare these two eyes, for I still hope to see my Beloved.
Your line: spare the eyes. Today, when the day pecks at you, keep one thing safe: the part of you still looking for good. Day two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Farid's saloks of longing, including the crow couplet, are sung in Sikh kirtan and are among the best-known lines of early Punjabi poetry.

original.note: Gurmukhi: naina, eyes; e due nainaa, these two eyes, the one thing Farid asks to keep.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome poem about crows and death.
what it means: let life take what it takes, but keep the eyes that are still looking, in hope, for the Beloved.
what a scholar hears: Saloks Farid 90–91, Ang 1382; pir (beloved, husband) and aas (hope) carry the Sufi bridal imagery; karang is a skeleton or carcass.
